periods.activity_title: Kites in the Sky: Activating Wonder and Reading Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.141): paired oral warm-up — kite experiences and observations.
Let us read (p.141): picture-based fill-in sentences using given word bank.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading oral warm-up from “Let us read” (p.141): invite students to share whether they have flown or watched a kite, describing its colours, shape, and tail. Take two or three brief responses to build a sense of shared experience before the poem is heard.

Read the poem “The Kites” aloud at an unhurried pace, with students following in their textbooks (p.141–143). Read it a second time, pausing after each stanza so students can absorb the imagery of kites like coloured birds and the child’s wish to drift on paper wings.

Turn to the picture-based activity in “Let us read” (p.141): students complete the five fill-in sentences using the word bank (windy, kite, flying, birds, sky, looking, has ribbons), then share two open responses — “If I were the child” and “If I were the kite” — aloud with a partner. Take whole-class feedback on the imaginative responses.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may conflate the poem’s fantasy (the child wishing to ride the kite) with literal kite-flying; steer the warm-up responses toward noticing the poem’s playful imagination, not just personal memory. The picture-task word bank is on p.141; ensure every student has the textbook open to that page before the activity begins.

periods.activity_title: True, False and the Poet’s Similes: Reading Closely

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.143): mark eleven statements True or False after silent reading.
Let us discuss (p.143–144): complete simile sentences and discuss their effect.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.145): answer any two ECR questions in writing.

time_bands.activity: Students read the poem silently for a quick, independent pass, keeping the True/False task in mind. Ask them to mark lightly in pencil as they read.

Work through the eleven True/False statements from “Let us discuss” (p.143) as a whole-class discussion: a student gives a verdict, and the class agrees or challenges by citing the exact stanza. Pay particular attention to items about weather (rainy day) and kite material (cloth and plastic), where the poem contradicts casual assumption.

Move to the simile activity in “Let us discuss” (p.143–144): students complete the two gapped sentences about “like coloured birds” and “light as air,” then share in pairs whether the similes help them imagine more vividly. Invite two or three pairs to voice their reasoning before the class.

periods.teacher_notes: When discussing similes, draw students’ attention to the poem’s appreciation note: the simile “like coloured birds” ties the kites visually to living, soaring things, while “light as air” makes the child’s wish physically conceivable. Students who say similes do not help should be asked which specific image they would replace, keeping the discussion text-anchored. Homework on p.145 extends thinking about the poet’s perspective without requiring class time.

periods.activity_title: Alliteration, Repetition and Rhyme: How Sound Makes the Poem Fly

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.144): find alliteration in stanzas 1 and 3; spot repeated words in the final stanza.
Let us think and reflect (p.144–145): circle the word unlike ‘fun’ and identify which line places the speaker above.

time_bands.activity: Guide students through the alliteration hunt in “Let us discuss” (p.144): they locate “wind-whipped” in stanza 1 and “wild wind” in stanza 3, name the consonant sound each pair shares, and then brainstorm four fresh alliterative word sets of their own in notebooks. Share examples aloud.

Ask students to read the final stanza aloud together and identify the two repeated words. Discuss briefly why the poet writes “high, high” rather than just “very high,” connecting repetition to the feeling of soaring elevation that the poem’s appreciation notes.

Work through “Let us think and reflect” (p.144–145): students circle the word that does not share the feeling of “fun” and identify the line that tells us the speaker was looking from above. Take class responses and close by asking students to read the fourth stanza aloud with expression to feel the aerial perspective.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often miss that “care” is the odd word because joy, excitement, and happiness all cluster around the poem’s tone of exhilarated play; nudge them to think about emotional register rather than dictionary meaning. The poem appreciation notes that the ABCB rhyme scheme and the four-line stanzas give the poem a lightness that mirrors the kites — drawing students’ attention to that pattern during the rhyme-study will enrich their sense of how form and content work together.

periods.activity_title: Listening to the Kite Festival and Sharing a Personal Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.148–149): circle incorrect words in seven statements and write correct words after two hearings.
Let us speak (p.149): share a kite-flying or kite-watching experience in complete sentences.

time_bands.activity: Briefly orient students: they will hear a short talk about the Kite Festival in India. Ask them to hold their pens and listen to the whole passage once before marking anything.

Read the Kite Festival transcript (p.163) aloud at a natural, clear pace for the first listening; students listen without writing. Read it again; this time students circle the incorrect words in the seven statements on p.148–149 and write the corrections. Confirm answers together: “January” for June, “Western” for Eastern, “Rajasthan” for Maharashtra, and “Independence Day” for Earth Day.

Move to “Let us speak” (p.149): each student prepares for a brief moment, then shares their kite-flying or kite-watching experience with the class in complete sentences, covering where, when, why, and how. Invite four or five speakers; encourage the rest to ask one follow-up question each.

periods.teacher_notes: When students report the corrections, insist they read out the full corrected sentence — not just the replacement word — so the habit of scanning the whole statement forms. During speaking, students who have never flown a kite should be told that watching kites fly is an equally valid experience; the poem’s opening stanza — “See the kites fly” — is itself an observer’s view, which gives shy responders an easy entry point.

periods.activity_title: I Am a Kite: Planning, Drafting and Peer Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.149): plan and draft a 100-word paragraph ‘I am a Kite’ using pair-discussion hints.

time_bands.activity: In pairs, students talk through all seven hints from “Let us write” (p.149): shape, colours, favourite parts, location, owner, activities, friends, and a message for humans. Each student jots two or three words against each hint as a planning skeleton before writing.

Students write their individual paragraph of about 100 words, titled “I am a Kite,” using the planning notes as a scaffold. Encourage first-person voice throughout and remind them to include at least one message for humans, as the prompt asks.

Pairs swap drafts for a quick peer read: the reader circles one image or idea they found vivid and one sentence they found unclear. Writers make a brief revision on the spot. Two volunteers read their final paragraph aloud to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Students tend to list the hints in order without shaping them into flowing prose; show a sample opening on the board — “I am a bright diamond-shaped kite, tugging at my string over the rooftop” — to model how a descriptive detail and a location can combine in one sentence. The poem’s imaginative leap — the child riding paper wings — is a useful mental model: encourage students to write from inside the kite’s experience, not just about it.
materials: Notebooks or loose sheets for drafting

periods.activity_title: Parts, Movement Words and a Cinquain: Building Kite Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.146): fill blanks in a conversation using parts-of-a-kite vocabulary.
Let us learn (p.148): circle drift-movement words; study glide, dive, soar, swoop, circle.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.147): compose a personal cinquain poem following the five-line structure.

time_bands.activity: Display the labelled kite diagram from “Let us learn” (p.146) and name each part together: nose, spine, cover, kite line, tail, reel. Students then complete the gapped conversation between Bina and Saroj in their textbooks, using the part names they have just reviewed.

Turn to the movement-word activity on p.148: students circle the words from the list (slow, fast, quick, upward, downward, round and round, float) that match “drift,” then study glide, dive, soar, swoop, and circle and describe in one phrase the kind of movement each suggests. Take whole-class responses and write the movement words on the board.

Introduce the cinquain structure from p.147 using the model poem: Kite / pretty, colourful / flying, floating, soaring / quickly, happily / paper-bird. Point out how line 3 uses exactly three action words from the movement-word set just studied. Set the cinquain composition as homework, asking students to choose any topic they like.

periods.teacher_notes: A common confusion: students include “fast” or “quick” as drift words — use the poem’s phrase “drift upon the paper wings” to show that drift implies a slow, unhurried movement, which excludes fast and quick. When presenting the cinquain model, note that line 5 requires a synonym (paper-bird for kite), not a description; asking students to brainstorm synonyms first prevents the most frequent error.
materials: Board or chart for movement-word list

periods.activity_title: Kites Across Time: Exploring Types, History and Making Your Own

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.149–150): identify common kite types and plan steps for making a kite.

time_bands.activity: Share the historical note from “Let us explore” (p.149): kites appear in the poetry of the thirteenth-century Marathi saint Namadeva, who called them “gudi” and noted they were made from kaagad (paper). Invite a quick class discussion on how old this tradition is and what it tells us about Indian culture.

Display or describe the five kite types from p.150: Parafoil, Delta, Rokkaku, Diamond-shaped, and Box kite. Students discuss in pairs which type is most commonly seen in their area and give a reason. Take class responses; note that the diamond-shaped kite is the type most associated with the festival tradition Namadeva described.

Students work through the kite-making planning task from p.150: using the steps available in the textbook or on a printed reference, each student lists the steps in order in their notebook and then begins folding and shaping a simple paper kite using the materials provided. Those who finish early write a short message on their kite, as the textbook suggests.

periods.teacher_notes: Bring pre-cut paper sheets, string or thread, and a thin stick or straw so students can follow the kite-making steps within the time available; without these materials, the hands-on task cannot run. Students who have studied the poem’s note that kites are made from paper will appreciate the connection to Namadeva’s kaagad — make that link explicit.
materials: Markers or crayons for kite messages

items.item_stem: Read the opening lines of the poem beginning “Up in the air” and answer the question. Which simile does the poet use in the first stanza to describe the kites, and what quality of the kites does it highlight?

options.label: A
options.text: The kites are compared to coloured birds, highlighting how they move and look as they soar.

options.label: B
options.text: The kites are compared to paper wings, highlighting the material they are made from.

options.label: C
options.text: The kites are compared to rooftops, highlighting how high they fly above the town.

options.label: D
options.text: The kites are compared to the wild wind, highlighting their speed and noise.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student confuses the simile vehicle (birds) with the noun that follows in a later stanza (paper wings), suggesting a misreading of stanza 1.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have recalled the phrase ‘wild wind’ from stanza 3 and mistakenly applied it to the stanza 1 comparison.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student inverted the poem’s spatial relationship: the kites fly above the rooftops, not alongside them.

items.item_stem: The final stanza of the poem ends with the words “high, high in the air.” Why does the poet repeat the word “high,” and how does this repetition connect to the overall emotional tone of the poem? Write your answer in two to three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The poet repeats “high” to emphasise how far above the ground the imagined child is, making the feeling of elevation vivid and dramatic. This repetition reflects the poem’s exhilarated, playful tone — the child’s delight in being envied by those far below is intensified by the soaring sense the doubled word creates.

items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read a short talk about the Kite Festival in India. Listen carefully. Then read the three statements below and write True or False for each, giving one reason drawn from what you heard.
1. The Kite Festival in India takes place during the month of January.
2. The festival called Uttarayan is celebrated mainly in Eastern India.
3. People in India also fly kites on Independence Day.

options.text: People in India also fly kites on Independence Day.
The festival called Uttarayan is celebrated mainly in Eastern India.
The Kite Festival in India takes place during the month of January.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the talk says the festival takes place during Makar Sankranti in the month of January.
2. False — the talk says Uttarayan is celebrated in Western India, not Eastern India.
3. True — the talk states that people across India fly kites to celebrate Independence Day.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to an informational talk, identifies inaccuracies, and self-corrects by matching heard content against written statements.
items.source_context: Spoken account of India’s Kite Festival: Makar Sankranti, Uttarayan, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Punjab, Independence Day.
items.item_stem: After listening to the talk about India’s Kite Festival, answer the following question in two to three sentences: The talk mentions several states where kite flying is celebrated. Name any two of those states and describe what you learned about how or when kites are flown there.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Any two of the following are acceptable: Gujarat, where Uttarayan is the main celebration during Makar Sankranti; Rajasthan, which also celebrates Uttarayan; Karnataka, where the Tourism Department organises the Kite Festival once each year; Punjab, which celebrates kite flying during Baisakhi and Basant Panchami. Students should name the state and give the specific occasion or organiser mentioned in the talk.

items.item_stem: Match each part of a kite in Column A with its correct description in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A (Part) | Column B (Description) |
|---|---|
| Nose | The long, flowing strip attached at the bottom end |
| Tail | The framework stick running down the centre |
| Spine | The string wound around a handheld holder |
| Reel | The pointed tip at the very top of the kite |
| Cover | The flat surface material stretched over the frame |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Nose – The pointed tip at the very top of the kite; Tail – The long, flowing strip attached at the bottom end; Spine – The framework stick running down the centre; Reel – The string wound around a handheld holder; Cover – The flat surface material stretched over the frame.

items.item_stem: The poem uses the word “drift” to describe how the child would move on the kite’s paper wings. Choose any two of the movement words below — glide, soar, dive, swoop — and write one sentence each showing how they describe a different type of movement from drifting. Your sentences may involve a kite, a bird, or anything that moves through the air.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Acceptable responses contrast the slow, unhurried quality of drift with a distinct movement quality for each chosen word. For example: “The kite began to soar rapidly upward as the wind grew stronger” (soar = rising swiftly); “The eagle dived steeply toward the ground” (dive = a sharp downward movement). Full credit for any two sentences that demonstrate understanding of the movement distinction.

items.source_context: Namadeva’s thirteenth-century gudi; five kite types (Parafoil, Delta, Rokkaku, Diamond, Box); kite-making steps and message.
items.item_stem: Look at the descriptions of five types of kites: Parafoil (no rigid frame, inflated by wind), Delta (triangular, single central spine), Rokkaku (six-sided, used in kite battles), Diamond (the most common, four-sided with a tail), Box kite (three-dimensional rectangular frame). Write a short paragraph of three to four sentences explaining which type you think is most commonly seen in India during the Kite Festival and why, using at least one detail about its shape or structure in your answer.

expected_elements: Names the Diamond-shaped kite (or gives a reasoned alternative).
Describes one structural feature (four-sided, has a tail, etc.).
Links the choice to cultural or practical reasons.
Writes in connected sentences with a clear concluding statement.

items.item_stem: The Kite Festival has deep roots in Indian history — the thirteenth-century Marathi poet Namadeva called the kite a “gudi” and wrote that it was made from “kaagad” (paper). Design a project plan in which you: (a) find out at least three steps needed to make a simple paper kite, (b) decide on a message you would write on your finished kite and explain why you chose it, and (c) describe how you would present your kite to your class. Write your plan in a short note of about 80 words.

expected_elements: Lists at least three kite-making steps in logical order.
States a specific message and explains its significance.
Describes the presentation to class clearly.
Connects the project to the cultural tradition mentioned in the chapter.
